topicName: Advanced Indexing: Columnstore, Filtered, and Included Columns
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Advanced Indexing in Microsoft SQL Server: Columnstore, Filtered, and Included Columns"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"As databases grow in scale and complexity, standard B-tree indexes often fall short of meeting performance requirements for both transactional workloads and heavy analytics. Microsoft SQL Server provides advanced indexing strategies to tackle these challenges. This tutorial explores Columnstore indexes for analytical queries, Filtered indexes for selective data ranges, and Included columns for avoiding key lookups."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Columnstore Indexes"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Traditional indexes store data in rows (Rowstore), which is efficient for OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) operations like seek and singleton inserts. However, analytical workloads (OLAP) typically scan millions of rows to aggregate a few columns. Columnstore indexes store data logically as a table with rows and columns, but physically store the data in column data compression segments. This drastically reduces I/O and leverages batch mode execution."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"CREATE CLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX IX_FactSales_Columnstore ON FactSales;"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can also combine rowstore and columnstore in SQL Server using Nonclustered Columnstore Indexes (NCCI), which allow you to index a transactional table for reporting without converting the entire table format."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"CREATE NONCLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX IX_Orders_NCCI ON Orders (OrderID, OrderDate, TotalAmount);O"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Filtered Indexes"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"A filtered index is a specialized nonclustered index optimized for queries that select a small percentage of rows from a table. It uses a filter predicate to index a portion of the rows in the table. This reduces index maintenance overhead, lowers index storage costs, and improves query performance by keeping index statistics accurate and compact."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_ActiveOrders ON Orders (CustomerID, OrderDate) WHERE Status = 'Active';"},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Reduced Storage: Only rows matching the predicate are stored in the index structure."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Lower Maintenance: Updates to rows that do not match the filter do not cause index page splits or updates."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Query Match Requirement: The query optimizer will only use the filtered index if the query predicate matches the index filter expression."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Included Columns"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"When creating a nonclustered index, you can add non-key columns to the leaf level of the index using the INCLUDE clause. This allows you to cover queries completely within the index structure, preventing the storage engine from performing costly 'Key Lookups' (or RID lookups on heap tables) back to the base table to retrieve missing columns."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Employees_Department ON Employees (DepartmentID) INCLUDE (FirstName, LastName, Email);"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"In the example above, DepartmentID is part of the B-tree key, while FirstName, LastName, and Email reside exclusively in the leaf nodes. This keeps the B-tree levels compact while still satisfying queries that select those specific employee details."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary and Best Practices"},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Columnstore indexes for large data warehouses, reporting tables, and historical data archives needing high aggregation performance."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Filtered indexes to optimize queries against sparse data, active status flags, or specific high-value subsets."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Included columns to eliminate expensive Key Lookups without exceeding the SQL Server maximum key size limit (900 bytes)."}]
